cards.text: For seven days and seven nights, Job's three friends have sat on the ground with him, and nobody has said a word. Job's covered in boils, and his own wife told him, “Curse God and die!” After this, Job finally opens his mouth.

cards.question: Job's wife told him to curse God. When Job finally opens his mouth, what does he curse?

cards.text: Job says, “May the day of my birth perish, and the night it was said, ‘A boy is conceived.’” Friend, most people want a party on their birthday, and Job wants his to PERISH.

cards.question: Job wants the day he was born undone. He wishes that day had turned to ___.
Job asks God above to shine a bright light on the day he was born so it's remembered.

cards.text: Job keeps piling it on: darkness and gloom, a cloud settling over that day, blackness to overwhelm it. That's not asking for a little shade, friend, that's ordering the FULL blackout package.
Then he goes after the night too. Job says, “If only darkness had taken that night away!”

cards.question: Job wants the night he was conceived taken away. Where does he never want that night to appear?

answers.text: Among the days of the year
Among the songs of the people
Among the records of the kings

cards.question: Job wants the night he was conceived to be full of joyful voices.

cards.text: He even wants that night cursed by those who curse the day, the ones prepared to rouse Leviathan. Friend, when you're calling in people who wake up Leviathan, this is NOT a strongly worded email.

cards.question: Job wants that night's morning stars to go dark, and he wants the night to wait in vain for ___.
Job finally says why he's cursing the night he was conceived. What's his reason?

answers.text: It did not hide sorrow from his eyes
It was when his flocks were taken
It was when the boils first came

cards.text: Job's cursed the day and he's cursed the night. Now the why questions start, and the first one is a heavy one: why didn't he die the moment he was born?
Why were there knees to receive him, and someone there to nurse him? I think every bit of care he got as a baby feels like a question mark to him now.

cards.question: Job says that if he had died at birth, he'd be lying down right now. What would he have?
Job pictures himself at rest among those who have already died. Who does he say he'd be lying there with?

cards.text: Princes who had gold, houses filled with silver. Meanwhile the fanciest thing in my old junk drawer was a coupon that expired YEARS ago, and it still acted like royalty.

cards.question: Job says the kings and counselors lying at rest built cities that are still standing strong.

cards.text: Then Job asks why he wasn't hidden like a stillborn child, like an infant who never sees daylight. I spent years in a dark drawer, friend, but Job's dark is deeper than anything I ever knew.

cards.question: Job describes the place where the dead lie. What does he say the weary find there?
In that place where the dead lie, Job says captives still hear the voice of the oppressor.
Job says small and great are both in that place where the dead lie, and there the slave is ___ from his master.

cards.text: Then Job asks a bigger why, about more than just himself. Why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter of soul?

cards.question: Job describes miserable people who long for death that does not come. What does he say they search for it like?

cards.text: Those people rejoice when they reach the grave, Job says. Then he turns it back on himself: why is life given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?

cards.question: Job describes his days now. He says that when food is put before him, he ___.

cards.text: His groans pour out like water. I bet even the quiet in that place felt heavy.

cards.question: Job says the trouble he dreaded has stayed far away from him.

cards.text: Job ends with this: “I am not at ease or quiet; I have no rest, for trouble has come.” Job's said his piece, friend, but this story is a LONG way from over.

findings.problem: The card tells facts from Job 2: the three friends sitting with him seven days and seven nights without a word (2:13), the boils (2:7), and his wife's line "Curse God and die!" (2:9). But it cites only Job 3:1, so those facts have no reference.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Same issue under the personality rules: the Job 2 facts on this card carry no reference.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: Card 7 quotes the first half of 3:6. Card 8 then asks the baker to supply the rest of that line ("May it not appear among the days of the year"). That is guessing the next words, and the baker can't reason it out from anything told so far.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The question is about the night Job was conceived. The wrong answers (when his flocks were taken, when the boils first came) can't be true of that night, so they aren't believable and the baker rules them out without understanding 3:10. The right answer also sounds more like the Bible than the other two.

rule.text: For why and meaning questions, wrong answers only need to be believable.

findings.problem: The right answer ("It did not hide sorrow from his eyes") echoes the Bible's wording, while the two wrong answers are plain event descriptions. The right answer stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Company" can be argued right. The passage says small and great are both there (3:19) and that Job would lie with kings and counselors (3:14), so the dead are not alone in that place.

rule.text: A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The card asks for the exact simile in 3:21 ("like hidden treasure"). That is guessing the wording of the line, like the Psalm 23 anointing-oil example. Nothing earlier lets the baker reason to it, so getting it right is luck.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: "That place" is unclear. The last time it was used (cards 8–10), it meant the place where the dead lie, not Job's own days. "The quiet" also points against the text: Job's groans pour out like water (3:24), and he says he is "not at ease or quiet" (3:26). The moment doesn't make sense as written.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.
